content.title: ‘Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen’ Loses Steam: Review
content.text: Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen Could’ve Been a Classic By , a Vulture TV critic who also covers film and pop culture. She is a juror for the Peabody Awards. Light spoilers follow for Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen, which premiered with all eight episodes on Netflix on March 26. A woman with no family, a mysterious background, and a nearly clairvoyant sense of when things around her are turning cosmically wrong gets engaged to a rich, pedigreed, happy-go-lucky guy. There are deadly miscommunications among relatives, an injured animal that becomes a reflection of the wounded protagonist, and buckets of viscera. This is the kind of conflict setup any horror fan would recognize, but Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen rearranges it all in such a deft, inspired way that if this project were shorter and tighter, it would be a classic of the genre. Created by Haley Z. Boston, who worked on the Netflix horror series Brand New Cherry Flavor and Guillermo del Toro’s Cabinet of Curiosities, and produced by the Duffer Brothers, Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen follows Rachel (Camila Morrone) and Nicky (Adam DiMarco) in the days leading up to their wedding. They met in an airport three years ago when Rachel refused to board her flight because of a bad feeling and Nicky believed her warning. Instead, they drove together from Austin to Chicago and fell in love along the way. Morrone plays Rachel as a woman who can’t quite believe her luck and keeps touching her partner to check that he’s real. Here’s this guy who gets her, who accepts her for whatever sixth sense she may possess, and she’s so charmed by that love — so overwhelmed by it — that she accepts his proposal despite her previous hesitations about marriage. Now they’re on another road trip, this time to Nicky’s family’s Frank Lloyd Wright–style mansion in the woods, where they will wed despite no one from Rachel’s side attending; her parents are out of the picture. In the days before the ceremony, Rachel meets Nicky’s relatives, most important his mom, Victoria (Jennifer Jason Leigh); sister Portia (Gus Birney); and older brother, Jules (Jeff Wilbusch). All of them have heard such nice things about her but, on a baseline level, view her as an outsider. Their family unit has the kind of protectively constrictive tightness that comes from wealth, and Rachel, with her black nail polish, tattoos, and constant weed smoking, may not make the cut. As frustrating as it is that Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen opens with Rachel and Nicky’s wedding, then flashes back to “five days until ‘I do’” instead of being confident enough to tell a linear story, its cold open is the high point. The series is most immersive when it leans into the tension between society telling Rachel she has made the right choice and her body screaming at her that something is wrong; this claustrophobic, paranoid jolt emphasizes how much walking down the aisle can feel like an invitation to be judged, assessed, and sized up as prey or product. When the camera captures Rachel’s perspective looking down the aisle toward Nicky waiting for her at the altar, the guests’ chatter muffles and her breathing grows louder. The lighting is desaturated, the room shadowy, the attendees’ expressions inscrutable, even antagonistic. An unearthly growl rises in the sound mix and then the series cuts from a shot of Nicky readying himself to slide a gold band onto Rachel’s finger to hallways elsewhere in the house coated in blood. In that mode of atmospheric grimness and allusive dread, the series is agonizingly, horrendously tense, so much so that I couldn’t finish the premiere at night and had to watch the show exclusively during the day. Rachel and Nicky’s nuptials spark the narrative, but the series is most interested in the concept of a soul mate and how to stretch that idea to its literal extreme, and it slyly maneuvers its characters to explore tension within seemingly perfect relationships. If their bond isn’t sincere, selfless, and motivated by each others’ happiness over their own, then something very bad is going to … well, you get the idea. Boston knows the genre classics and layers them so liberally in the season’s first half that there’s no chance to catch your breath: Unseen visitors rattle doorknobs, footsteps skitter down hallways, reflections in windows and mirrors don’t sync with reality, and splatters of bright-red blood contrast with the series’ otherwise aquarium-green palette. Like The Night House, The Invisible Man, or Rebecca, Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen has a strong sense of how to unite the classic idea of a haunted house with a more modern version of a gaslighting man. But eventually it stops being suggestive and starts getting explicit, and by hand-holding its audience, the series falters. We live in a time of worrisome media illiteracy, and the show’s decision to dive so fully into “What actually happened was …” pedantry both pads its runtime and deflates its spookiness. This is not a performance problem — Morrone is skilled at undercutting her cool-girl casualness with anxiety and avoidance, and Wilbusch develops Nicky’s older brother, Jules, from a bullying brat into an obviously wounded failson. (Also deserving of praise: whoever in the makeup department chose Morrone’s lipstick shades. They’re beautifully garish.) This is a pacing and writing problem, and the series’ last three episodes especially struggle to maintain momentum. They’re the season’s goriest installments, and while they feature an early contender for the year’s most arousing TV sex scene, they’re also, thematically, the series’ flattest. Thanks to an onslaught of overly clarifying dialogue, all the tension the series worked so hard to build dissipates, like a balloon slowly losing air until it slumps to the floor, unable to bear its own weight. That’s too bad because Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen begins as a riveting remix of female-focused horror’s greatest hits. Horror films have long mined women’s experiences to explore how societies view otherness and monstrosity — menstruation and puberty (Carrie, The Witch), sapphic relationships (Heavenly Creatures, The Neon Demon), and motherhood (The Babadook, Under the Shadow) — and Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen does something novel by adding marriage to that conversation. It’s so confident in its argument that sometimes the most foreboding thing about heteronormativity is how customs and rituals are enforced upon us that we may not fully understand, and if we did, we probably wouldn’t agree with them. There’s an antisocial wish fulfillment in watching Rachel kick against Nicky’s family’s “This is how we do things” properness and a fascinating, underdeveloped suggestion that maybe Rachel and another relative of Nicky’s are the pair actually fated to be together. Condense the series’ depiction of love and marriage as a roller-coaster ride of eyes-squeezed-shut faith and stomach-clenching doubt into a two-hour movie, and Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen would be cooking all the way through. As it is, it’s a nervy beginning, a badass final sequence, and many minutes of domestic blisslessness in between. An all-timer of a movie lurks inside Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen, and the spookiest thing is that it exists in this bloated form.
